mistakes.description: A leg is loose: a row keeps switching between connected and empty
mistakes.hint: One row keeps switching between connected and empty while I measure. That means a leg is loose. Find the row with the yellow light and push that leg in firmly, all the way down.
mistakes.explain: A leg that is not pushed all the way in only touches the metal clip some of the time, so that row keeps connecting and letting go. Push each leg in the yellow row firmly until it stops moving, then check again.

mini_lesson.title: Loose legs make blinking circuits
mini_lesson.idea: A part only works while its metal leg touches the metal clip inside the hole. A loose leg touches, then lets go, then touches again. So the circuit keeps switching on and off, like a lamp with a wobbly cord.
mini_lesson.question: A row keeps switching between connected and empty. What is the most likely reason?
options: A leg is loose in its hole
mini_lesson.why: When a leg wobbles in its hole, it keeps touching and letting go of the clip, so the row comes and goes.

mistakes.hint: The middle voltage is much lower than half of 3.3 volts. How the voltage splits depends on the sizes of the two resistors. Are they really the same size?
mistakes.explain: The bottom resistor is 1k (brown-black-red) instead of 10k (brown-black-orange). With 10k on top and 1k on the bottom, the middle gets only 1/11 of 3.3 volts, about 0.3 V. Use a 10k on the bottom too, so both match and the middle reads 1.65 V.

mini_lesson.title: Resistors share the voltage
mini_lesson.idea: Two resistors in a line share the voltage, like friends sharing a pizza. The bigger resistor gets the bigger share, just like the hungrier friend gets more slices. If both resistors are the same size, each one gets exactly half.
mini_lesson.question: Two resistors share 3.3 volts, and one is much bigger than the other. Which one gets more of the voltage?
options: They always get the same amount
mini_lesson.why: The bigger resistor always gets the bigger share of the voltage.

mistakes.description: Measuring row not connected to the middle, so the number jumps
mistakes.hint: The middle voltage keeps jumping around. That happens when the measuring row is not touching anything. Check the measuring row.
mistakes.explain: The measuring row is not connected to the middle, where the two resistors meet, so it measures nothing and the number drifts. Move the wire so the measuring row connects to the middle. The lit row shows the measuring row.

mini_lesson.title: Measure only what you touch
mini_lesson.idea: A measuring wire tells you the voltage of whatever it touches. If it touches nothing, it picks up random noise, like a radio stuck between stations. That noise makes the number jump around.
mini_lesson.question: Why would a voltage number keep jumping around?
options: The measuring row is not touching anything
The power supply is almost empty
mini_lesson.why: A wire that touches nothing picks up random noise instead of a real voltage.

mistakes.hint: The middle voltage is much higher than half of 3.3 volts. How the voltage splits depends on the sizes of the two resistors. Are they really the same size?
mistakes.explain: The top resistor is 1k (brown-black-red) instead of 10k (brown-black-orange). With 1k on top and 10k on the bottom, the middle gets 10/11 of 3.3 volts, about 3.0 V. Use a 10k on top too, so both match and the middle reads 1.65 V.

mini_lesson.title: Bigger resistor, bigger share
mini_lesson.idea: Going from 3.3 volts down to 0 is like walking down two sets of stairs. Each resistor is one set, and a bigger resistor has more steps, so it takes more of the height. The middle of the circuit is the landing between the two sets.
mini_lesson.question: Two sets of stairs go from 3.3 volts down to 0. Which set takes more of the height?
mini_lesson.why: More steps take more height, just like a bigger resistor takes more of the voltage.

mistakes.description: The bottom resistor or the ground wire may not be connected, or the top resistor may be much smaller than the bottom one (the board cannot tell which)
mistakes.hint: The middle row has the full 3.3 volts. Two things can do this, and the board cannot tell which. The current may not get from the middle down to ground. Or the top resistor may be much smaller than the bottom one. Look at every part between the middle and ground, and compare the color bands of the two resistors.
mistakes.explain: Two things can cause this, and the board cannot tell which. The bottom resistor may not be connected, or the ground wire may not reach it: then the loop is broken below the middle and the middle keeps the full 3.3 volts. Or the top resistor may be much smaller than the bottom one, for example 1k (brown-black-red) instead of 10k (brown-black-orange): then the middle gets almost all of the 3.3 volts, more than this board's meter can tell from the full 3.3. Both resistors should be 10k, and the bottom one should go from the middle row to the ground row.

mini_lesson.title: No flow, no voltage drop
mini_lesson.idea: A resistor only lowers the voltage when current flows through it. It is like a garden hose with the end blocked: no water flows, so the pressure is the same all along the hose. With no current, every point keeps the full push of the power supply.
mini_lesson.question: No current is flowing through a resistor. How much voltage does it take away?
mini_lesson.why: With no current, a resistor takes away no voltage, so the full push passes along.

mistakes.description: Top resistor (or the 3.3 V wire) may not be connected
mistakes.hint: No current is flowing, and the middle row has 0 volts. The middle seems to have no path to the 3.3 volt side. Look at every part between 3.3 V and the middle.
mistakes.explain: The top resistor may not be connected, or the 3.3 V wire may not reach it. Either way nothing joins the middle to 3.3 V, so no current flows and the middle sits at 0 volts. The top 10k resistor should go from the 3.3 V row to the middle row.

mini_lesson.title: Voltage needs a path from power
mini_lesson.idea: A row only gets voltage if it has a path back to the power supply. It is like a room that gets light only through one door: shut the door, and the room goes dark. A row that touches only ground stays at 0 volts.
mini_lesson.question: A row touches ground but has no path to the power supply. What voltage will it read?
mini_lesson.why: Without a path to the power supply, nothing pushes on that row, so it reads 0 volts.
